title: The goal
question: I want to generate text.
explanation: Instead of writing a whole sentence at once, I can grow it one small piece at a time. I start with some text, add a piece, then repeat.
caption: This is an illustration of growing text, not output from a running model.
next: To choose what to add, I need a way to guess what comes next.

title: The next guess
question: I need to guess the next character.
explanation: After “ca”, I might see “t”, “r”, or “n”. There is no single right answer for every situation. I need probabilities: numbers that say how likely each choice is.
caption: The possibilities depend on the text the model has seen.
next: First, I need to decide exactly what kind of piece I am predicting.

title: Tokens
question: I need to split text into pieces.
explanation: A token is one piece of text the model handles at a time. For our first model, each character is a token, including spaces. Larger language models often use pieces of words instead.
caption: Here, three characters make three tokens. We keep this rule for the rest of the journey.
next: Now I need a consistent way to identify each token in my calculations.

title: Token IDs
question: I give each token a number.
explanation: I make a vocabulary: a list of the tokens my model knows. Each gets a token ID, like a numbered seat. That lets me use it to look up counts and, later, learned numbers. The ID is a label, not a meaning or a score.
caption: We could renumber the vocabulary, as long as all our lookups stayed consistent.
next: With tokens identified, I can count which ones tend to follow each other.

title: Count patterns
question: I can make a first guess by counting.
explanation: Imagine a tiny collection containing “cat” six times, “car” three times, and “can” once. After “a”, I count six “t”s, three “r”s, and one “n”. Dividing by ten turns these counts into probabilities. This is already a very simple language model.
caption: These numbers come from the invented collection above. This baseline looks only at the previous character.
next: I will be working with lots of numbers together. There is a useful name for an ordered list of them.

title: Vectors
question: I can keep related numbers in a list.
explanation: A vector is an ordered list of numbers. For example, I can store the probabilities of “t”, “r”, and “n” as [0.6, 0.3, 0.1]. Each position has a known job. Change the order without changing the labels, and the list means something different.
caption: This vector holds probabilities. Other vectors can hold other kinds of numbers.
next: To build a more flexible model, I also want an adjustable vector for each token.

title: Embeddings
question: I give each token a learnable vector.
explanation: An embedding is a vector the model learns for a token. The token ID tells me which vector to look up. Instead of doing arithmetic on arbitrary ID numbers, the model works with these adjustable values to build predictions.
caption: These three values are made up. Real embedding values start from an initialization and change during training. They are not percentages or hand-written labels like “animal” or “plural”.
next: A token alone still tells me very little. I need to consider the surrounding text.

title: Context & attention
question: I need more than the last character.
explanation: “The cat” and “a hat” both end in “t”, so our counting model gives them the same next guess. A richer model uses earlier tokens too. Attention combines information from their vectors using learned weights. Position information tells the model which token came where.
caption: When predicting what follows a position, the model can use tokens up to that position, never the future answer. Attention is a way to combine context, not a guarantee of understanding.
next: The embeddings and attention contain adjustable numbers. How do those numbers become useful?

title: Learning
question: I improve the numbers with practice.
explanation: I show the model a piece of real text, ask it to predict the next token, and compare its probabilities with the token that actually followed. A loss measures how poorly it predicted that token. Training makes small changes to the model’s numbers to reduce this loss, over many examples.
caption: Embeddings and the other model weights learn together. I also check predictions on text kept out of training: memorizing the examples is not enough.
next: Once trained, I can keep those numbers fixed and use the model to write.

title: Generate
question: I choose a token, then do it again.
explanation: The trained model gives me probabilities for the next token. I sample one: a more likely token has a greater chance of being chosen. I add it to the text and predict again using the updated context. Repeating this loop generates text.
caption: The text changes during generation; the trained weights stay fixed. A small model may produce nonsense—it has learned patterns, not guaranteed facts.
next: That is the core journey: text becomes tokens, tokens become numbers, practice improves predictions, and repeated predictions become text.
